title: An Abandoned Family Dollar Became a Free Store — With a Roller Rink Inside
summary:
The old Family Dollar in New Orleans' Lower Ninth Ward still has graffiti on its walls. It looks abandoned. But twice a week, people line up outside — and when the doors open, they rush in to grab clothing, toys, food, books, and household goods. Everything is free.

Dan Bingler, 42, started the New Orleans Free Store three years ago. He made a deal with the property owner to use the 9,000-square-foot building rent-free, paying only utilities. The owner keeps the property maintained until he's ready to redevelop it. "It's just a crazy opportunity," Bingler says. He thinks the idea could be copied in empty storefronts across the country.

Bingler runs the Greater New Orleans Caring Collective, a mutual-aid group. He started organizing grocery deliveries during the Covid-19 pandemic, and after Hurricane Ida hit Louisiana in 2021, donations poured in. "People who are struggling don't just want the bare necessities," he says. "They want nice things, too, because they deserve nice things, too."

Ernestine Lane shops there with a friend from church. "They see the graffiti on the outside of the building and it's a misconception," she says. "I say, 'Go in, there's blessings in there, go in.'"

Hilsa Rodriguez, a mom of six, shops with her stepdaughters Angela, 8, and Gloria, 9. Angela found animal-print hair clips for school; Gloria picked out a furry vest to give to a baby her stepmom babysits. "To have all the donations that they have here," Rodriguez says, "we're very grateful."

The store also hosts free STI testing, food handouts, basic medical care, art classes, and punk shows. On Wednesday nights, the lights dim and the polished concrete floor becomes a roller rink. Chrishana Simon, who learned to skate there, glides around in a furry trapper hat with headphones over it. The store is open to anyone, and everything inside is free.
why_it_matters: A free store tests an idea that reaches far beyond one neighbourhood: that empty buildings, donated goods and volunteer time can meet real needs without money changing hands, and that people in struggling areas deserve quality things rather than leftovers. If the model spreads, it could change how cities treat abandoned retail space — and what counts as a safety net.

background_read: The Lower Ninth Ward is a neighbourhood in New Orleans (a large city in Louisiana, in the southern United States) that was badly flooded when Hurricane Katrina struck in 2005, and it has struggled to rebuild since.

Family Dollar is a chain of discount shops found across the US; the company has closed hundreds of stores in recent years, leaving empty buildings behind, especially in poorer neighbourhoods where the nearest place to buy food may be a dollar store or a petrol station.
Hurricane Ida (a powerful storm that hit Louisiana in 2021) knocked out power for days and damaged homes, and the donations that followed helped community groups like Bingler's get started.

Mutual aid is an old idea: instead of waiting for the government or a charity to help, neighbours collect and share what they have — a practice that spread widely during the Covid-19 pandemic, when many people lost work.

Empty shops like this one often sit unused for years while owners wait for land prices to rise, so a rent-free deal lets a community put the space to use right now; similar free stores and 'free fridges' have appeared in other US cities.

perspectives.description: Hilsa Rodriguez, a mother of six, can pick up hair clips for school and a gift for a baby without spending money, and Ernestine Lane calls the store 'blessings.' The space also offers medical testing, food handouts and art classes, turning a symbol of neighbourhood decline into something genuinely useful.

The store exists only because a landlord is waiting to redevelop, and it runs on donations, volunteers and one man's deal rather than stable funding. It can vanish the moment the property is sold, and relying on charity for basics can let governments and companies off the hook for the poverty that makes such stores necessary.

Neighbour-run mutual aid has repeatedly filled gaps during crises, from the Covid-19 pandemic to Hurricane Ida, while official relief moves slowly. Discount chains expanded quickly into low-income areas and then closed hundreds of stores, leaving shells that communities now improvise with — a pattern of reuse rather than a one-off.

Bingler argues the idea could be copied in empty storefronts nationwide, but open questions remain: whether a volunteer-run store survives its founder, whether cities would change rules to make lending vacant buildings easier, and whether 'free' can grow beyond a handful of neighbourhoods.
